To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
both normal mucosal and tumor RTL are related to disease severity in patients with colorectal cancer, but not to disease outcome.

(i) telomere length in normal mucosa and colorectal cancer (cRTL) are both associated with tumor stage and cRTL is also associated with CIN profiles in colorectal carcinomas, (ii) normal mucosa RTL is independently associated with female gender, proximal cancer location, and the TERT G allele, (iii) cRTL is not related to germline telomere length variants, MSI, CIMP or KRAS, BRAFF or TP53 mutation
normal tissue and tumor RTL are related to CRC progression and chromosome instability, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of telomere biology in CRC development and progression.
the relationship of normal mucosa and cancer tissue telomere lengths to disease progression and prognosis in colorectal cancer patients.
the relationship of normal and cancer telomere lengths to CRC progression, and highlights divergent associations of tumor telomere length and CIN profiles in CRC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
telomere shortness and lengthening are both associated with colorectal carcinogenesis.
telomere shortness in the normal tissue is an independent risk factor for CRC, while telomere lengthening in CRCs is associated with near-tetraploid karyotype and more chromosome breaks.
normal and tumor telomeres lengthen with age and disease progression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

telomere lengths of both normal mucosa (age-related telomere shorting) and cancer tissue (telomere shortening or lengthening) are related to disease stage and CIN status, but neither normal mucosa telomere length, nor cancer tissue telomere length are associated with prognosis.
the relative telomere lengths of both normal and tumor tissue are independently associated with colorectal cancer progression, but not with clinical outcomes.
normal mucosa and cancer telomere length are associated with disease progression and chromosome stability in colorectal cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the telomere biology of both normal mucosa (and presumably stem cells) and cancer is important for understanding CRC progression and prognosis.
telomere length is a biomarker for colorectal cancer risk and progression.
normal mucosa and cancer telomere length may serve as prognostic markers for CRC progression and prognosis.
